solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Jean-Paul Sartre's deep discomfort?

parts.note: a Frenchman would name the discomfort felt on the deep (the sea) in his own language: literally 'sickness of the sea'

explanation.surface: A wry question about the existential anguish of the French philosopher Sartre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deep discomfort' suggests philosophical angst, but the deep is the sea, and the French phrase for seasickness is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase is used in English too as a name for seasickness, nausea brought on by a ship's motion.

clue.text: Sabotaged agenda about Oxford course — not an essential item

indicators.note: the shuffled letters go around the other piece, enclosing it
something sabotaged is wrecked, so the letters of the word after it are thrown into a new order

parts.note: PPE, Philosophy, Politics and Economics, is a famous Oxford degree course

explanation.surface: A meeting's agenda has been wrecked over a discussion of an Oxford course deemed inessential.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sabotaged' signals the rearrangement and 'about' the enclosure; Oxford's PPE degree is the course meant.
explanation.definitionFit: An appendage is an attached extra, something added on that the main body could do without.

clue.text: Pole angry about everything and nothing

indicators.note: about signals turning round, so the two pieces before it are read backwards

parts.note: N is the north pole
mad means angry
all means everything

explanation.surface: A Polish man is furious about everything, yet the clue ends on nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' is not a Polish person but a magnetic pole; 'about' turns N MAD into DAMN.
explanation.definitionFit: Damn all is an informal idiom meaning nothing whatsoever.

clue.text: Honourable man wasting time

indicators.note: wasting time suggests the time is thrown away, so that letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: a mortal is a human being, a man as opposed to a god

explanation.surface: An upright man is criticised for frittering away his hours.
explanation.definitionFit: A moral person acts on principle, so the adjective is a synonym of upright and honourable.

clue.text: Endless fish brought up, caught with this?

indicators.note: in a down answer, brought up means read from bottom to top, so the letters are reversed
without its end means the final letter is dropped

parts.note: the dory is a sea fish (John Dory)

explanation.surface: An angler's riddle: a fish is landed, and what was it caught with?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' cuts DORY to DOR; 'brought up' turns it over in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglers catch fish using a rod, the long flexible pole carrying the line.

clue.text: Group that's very large including agents abroad

indicators.note: including means the first piece holds the second inside it

parts.note: so means very, as in so good
L is the clothing abbreviation for large
the CIA is the American intelligence agency, whose agents work abroad

explanation.surface: A huge organisation counts foreign spies among its members.
explanation.walkthrough: 'very large' looks like one idea but gives two separate pieces; 'including' signals the enclosure.
explanation.definitionFit: A social is a gathering of club members or a community, a group meeting for company.

clue.text: Writer of Rocket Man, did you say?

indicators.note: a query about what was said signals that the word must sound like the one meant

parts.note: George Stephenson built the Rocket, the famous early steam locomotive

explanation.surface: Someone asks if a writer was behind the Elton John song Rocket Man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocket Man' looks like the song but means the engineer Stephenson, whose name is pronounced like the author's.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote Treasure Island and Kidnapped, so he is a famous author.

clue.text: Solicit a delegate guarding stronghold

indicators.note: words guarding something hold it within them, so the answer is concealed in the run of letters

explanation.surface: Someone canvasses a delegate who protects a fortress.
explanation.definitionFit: A citadel is a fortress that commands a city, a stronghold of last resort.

clue.text: Quarrel? It's a right ding-dong!

parts.note: a ding-dong is British slang for a noisy row or argument

explanation.surface: An argument is described as a proper slanging match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quarrel' seems to mean a row, but here it is the bolt fired from a crossbow.
explanation.definitionFit: A quarrel is the short heavy bolt shot from a crossbow, a kind of arrow.

clue.text: On way back, plans to get something to eat

indicators.note: going back means the letters are read in reverse order

parts.note: maps are plans or charts

explanation.surface: A traveller on the return journey plans a meal stop.
explanation.definitionFit: Spam is a brand of tinned luncheon meat, so it is food.

clue.text: Yours truly surrounded by Bolshevik's dogs

indicators.note: surrounded by means the first piece sits within the second

parts.note: a Bolshevik is a Red; with the 's the word gives REDS
the setter of the puzzle refers to themself

explanation.surface: The writer is hemmed in by a Russian revolutionary's hounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yours truly' means the crossword's setter, as is common in cryptics.
explanation.definitionFit: Red setters, or Irish setters, are a breed of gun dog with glossy red coats.

clue.text: Sound of final bell disturbed one within

indicators.note: within means the letter goes inside the rearranged letters
letters that are disturbed are knocked out of place and rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: The noise of the closing bell disturbs someone inside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like noise but is the definition, meaning reliable; 'disturbed' rearranges FINAL BELL, with I added 'within'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sound means reliable or valid, and infallible means incapable of error.

clue.text: Too much ale left undrunk? This suggests not

definitions.text: Too much ale left undrunk? This suggests not

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer

indicators.note: undrunk says the letter is not consumed, so it is left out of the word

parts.note: a glut is an excess, too much of something

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether too much beer has been left in the glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'undrunk' removes L from BEER GLUT; the whole clue then describes a paunch that proves no ale was left.
explanation.definitionFit: A beer gut is a large belly blamed on heavy drinking of beer.

clue.text: Drink in The Feathers?

definitions.meaning: to ... a drink is to swallow it quickly
the soft fine feathers of birds

explanation.surface: A drink at a pub called The Feathers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Feathers' looks like a pub name, a common one in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: To down is to gulp a drink, and down also names the soft plumage of young birds.

clue.text: Outspoken historian in border city

indicators.note: outspoken here means spoken out loud, so the word is one that sounds the same

parts.note: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, author of The French Revolution

explanation.surface: A frank historian lives in a city near a frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outspoken' seems to describe the historian's manner but signals the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Carlisle is the English city in Cumbria closest to the Scottish border.

clue.text: Bet on nuns somehow making baby's hat

indicators.note: somehow suggests the letters get arranged in some way or other

explanation.surface: Gambling on nuns is somehow linked to making an infant's headgear.
explanation.definitionFit: A sunbonnet is a brimmed cotton bonnet that shades a baby's face and neck from the sun.

clue.text: Big story about parking cut

indicators.note: about means the word goes around the other piece, enclosing it

parts.note: a slash is a cut
P is the abbreviation for parking on road signs

explanation.surface: A major news report concerns reductions in parking spaces.
explanation.definitionFit: In journalism a splash is a front-page lead story given big prominence.

clue.text: Might this way suit you?

parts.note: a street is a way, and this London street is where bespoke suits are tailored

explanation.surface: Someone politely asks if a suggested route is convenient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suit' reads as convenience, but means dressing a customer in a suit; Savile Row is London's street of bespoke tailors.
explanation.definitionFit: Savile Row is the London street famed for its tailors, whose shops literally suit people.

clue.text: Caretaker's relations not looking back

parts.note: sexual relations, so relations gives sex

indicators.note: looking back means the word is read in reverse

explanation.surface: A caretaker refuses to dwell on his past relationships.
explanation.definitionFit: A sexton is a church officer who looks after the building and churchyard, a church caretaker.

clue.text: Shuffle along after tango? Rubbish!

indicators.note: after places the walking word behind the letter for tango

parts.note: T is tango in the NATO phonetic alphabet
to waddle is to walk with short shuffling steps

explanation.surface: A dancer dismisses the idea of shuffling about after a tango.
explanation.definitionFit: Twaddle is silly, trivial talk, so it is an exclamation like nonsense.

clue.text: A case of English idiot interrupting play?

indicators.note: interrupting means breaking into the other word, so these letters go inside it

parts.note: give means slack or room to move, as in play in a rope
nit is British slang for a fool

explanation.surface: An English fool butting into a theatre performance becomes a court case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' is grammatical, not legal; 'play' is slack, not a drama.
explanation.definitionFit: The genitive is the grammatical case showing possession, as in Latin or the English 's.

clue.text: Screwed up Dickensian guy

parts.note: Oliver Twist is Dickens's best-known title character
Ed is a man's name, a guy

explanation.surface: A character from Dickens is described as warped.
explanation.definitionFit: Twisted means bent out of shape or warped in mind, as something screwed up is.

clue.text: Old man's code word for a pee

definitions.meaning: an old-fashioned word for father, one's old man
The NATO phonetic alphabet's word for the letter P

explanation.surface: An elderly man has a polite euphemism for going to the toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pee' here is the letter P spelled out, not the bodily function.
explanation.definitionFit: Papa means father, and in radio spelling the letter P is said as Papa.

clue.text: Cooker successfully installed on second occasion?

parts.note: an Aga is a British brand of heavy range cooker
in means elected or installed in office

explanation.surface: A new oven is fitted properly at the second attempt.
explanation.walkthrough: An Aga is a big cast-iron range cooker found in many British country kitchens.
explanation.definitionFit: Again means once more, on another occasion after the first.

clue.text: I set nobles up, it's pretended

indicators.note: up here means stirred up, so the letters are thrown into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone confesses to framing the aristocracy, though it is all a pretence.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostensible means apparent or professed, presented as true but possibly feigned.

clue.text: New husband coming off heroin? Such language!

indicators.note: coming off means leaving, so the letter is taken out of the word

parts.note: horse is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: A newly married man in drug withdrawal swears freely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Such language!' looks like disapproval of swearing, but simply defines a language.
explanation.definitionFit: Norse is the language of medieval Scandinavia, spoken by the Vikings.

clue.text: Plant's first appearance enthralling Henry

indicators.note: enthralling means holding captive, so these words hold the letter inside them

parts.note: a maiden voyage or speech is a first one
air means appearance or manner
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: A plant makes its debut and captivates someone called Henry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant's' gives the definition plus 's (is); 'first appearance' looks like one idea but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Maidenhair is a fern with delicate fronds, a common houseplant.

clue.text: Imbecile soldiers moving south

indicators.note: in a down answer, moving south means a letter goes lower, towards the end

parts.note: the SAS is the British army's Special Air Service

explanation.surface: Foolish troops are being transferred to the south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moving south' sends the first S of SAS to the bottom of this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An ass is a foolish person, a donkey being proverbially stupid.

clue.text: Having difficulty deciding end for Trueman?

definitions.meaning: pulled between two choices, unable to settle on one
a cryptic sense: the name has two ends, its first letter and its last, and this asks which of the two is meant

explanation.surface: Fred Trueman, the fast bowler, cannot choose which end to bowl from.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense reads the answer as T OR N, the two possible ends of Trueman. Fred Trueman was a famous English fast bowler, and bowlers choose an end.
explanation.definitionFit: Torn describes someone pulled two ways, unable to choose between options.

clue.text: Chuck out Austen novel

indicators.note: novel as an adjective means new, so the letters take a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone throws a Jane Austen novel away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book of Austen's but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To unseat someone is to remove them from a position, as an elected member is thrown out.

clue.text: Resign, being unhappy at blue-eyed boy's return?

indicators.note: at sets the mood word next to the other piece
return means coming back, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: a blue-eyed boy is a favourite, a pet; with 's it gives PETS
down means unhappy or low

explanation.surface: Someone quits, upset that the favourite has come back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns PETS into STEP.
explanation.definitionFit: To step down is to give up an office or post voluntarily, a phrasal synonym of resign.
